title: A Trust Is a Relationship, Not a Thing
summary: A trust is not a box that holds assets. It is a legal relationship in which one person holds property for the benefit of others, under duties the law enforces. Understand the three roles and what each can and cannot do, and every later trust decision becomes clearer.
body:
A trust is a relationship, not an object: one person owns property in law but must use it entirely for other people, and the law watches how they do it. Everything else about trusts follows from that sentence.

Recall

Q. What is a voidable or fraudulent transfer, in concept?

A. A transfer of assets that a court can set aside because it was made to defeat creditors, typically when the person was insolvent, about to be, or facing a known claim. Timing and intent are what courts examine, and the details vary by jurisdiction.

Q. What does key-person insurance protect?

A. The business, not the family. It pays the company if a person whose skill or relationships drive its value dies or is disabled, so the company can repay debt, hire a replacement or buy out an estate.

Q. Why do contemporaneous records carry more weight than later recollection?

A. Because they were made at the time, by people who did not yet know a dispute was coming. A note written the same day is evidence; a memory assembled two years later is argument.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer meets trusts in three places. First, as a planning tool: families use trusts to hold shares, land or investments for the next generation. Second, as a counterparty: you will buy land from a trust, borrow alongside one, or take investment from one. Third, as a trap: people sign documents as trustee without understanding that they have taken on personal, enforceable duties to other people. In all three places the question is the same. Who owns this, who benefits, and who answers for it? This week, I teach the concepts. The law of trusts differs between jurisdictions, and nothing here is a conclusion about any particular place. A real trust needs a lawyer who practises trust law where the trust is governed.

The three roles

Plain English first. A settlor is the person who creates the trust by handing property to someone else on terms. A trustee is the person who receives that property and holds legal title to it. A beneficiary is a person for whose benefit the property is held. Three roles, and the same human can sometimes hold more than one, but each role carries different rights.

The professional framing is that ownership is split in two. The trustee has the legal title: the trustee's name is on the share register or the land title, and the trustee signs contracts. The beneficiaries have the benefit: the right to have the property managed for them and, depending on the terms, to receive income or capital. In common law systems this split grew up in the courts of equity, which enforced the trustee's conscience when the ordinary law only saw the legal owner.

An applied example, hypothetical. A woman transfers 1,000,000 dollars of investments to her brother, to hold for her two children until the younger turns 25. She is the settlor. The brother is the trustee. The children are the beneficiaries. The brother's bank statement now shows the investments in his name, but he cannot spend a dollar on himself, cannot mix the money with his own, and must account to the children for every decision. If he buys himself a car with trust money, the children can sue him personally to restore it.

Say that out loud now.

What a trust is not

A trust is not, in most common law systems, a separate legal person in the way a corporation is. It does not usually sign contracts in its own name; the trustee does. This matters to you as a developer. When you buy land from "the Smith Family Trust", you are dealing with the trustees, and you need to see that they have the power under the trust deed to sell, that all of them who must sign do sign, and that any consent the deed requires has been given. A sale signed by one trustee when the deed requires two can be challenged later.

A trust is also not a way to keep control while appearing to give it away. If a settlor keeps the power to do whatever she likes with the property, a court or a tax authority may decide there was never a real trust at all, only a label. This is called a sham in some systems, and the test is whether the parties genuinely intended the trustee to hold the property on the stated terms. Substance over form, which we met in the tax weeks, applies here too.

A second applied example, hypothetical. A developer puts his shares in a holding company into a trust for his children, names himself sole trustee, keeps all the dividends, and tells his banker the shares are "in trust, so they are protected". The trust deed gives the beneficiaries nothing until he decides otherwise, and he decides everything. A creditor or a court may look through that arrangement and treat the shares as his. Calling something a trust does not change who really owns and controls it.

Why the trustee's duties are the whole point

The value of a trust to a family rests entirely on the trustee doing the job properly. The law therefore imposes duties on the trustee that are stricter than ordinary commercial duties. The trustee must act honestly, for the beneficiaries and not for himself, follow the terms of the deed, keep trust property separate, keep records, and invest prudently. We take those duties apart later this week, because most trust failures are duty failures, not drafting failures.

For a wealth builder this reframes the choice of trustee. You are not choosing a person you like. You are choosing who will be held to a fiduciary standard over your family's assets, possibly for decades, possibly after you have died. Competence, independence, availability and continuity matter more than warmth.

How the best do it

Professional trust companies do not rely on a single person's judgment. The common practice is a written investment policy for each trust, two signatures for any payment out, annual reviews of each beneficiary's circumstances, a minutes book recording every discretionary decision and the reasons for it, and a separation between the people who decide distributions and the people who move money. A small family can copy all of that: a written policy, two signatures, an annual meeting, and minutes. None of it requires a large firm. It requires the habit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a trust as a filing exercise: the deed is signed, the assets are transferred, and nobody behaves as a trustee afterwards. Decisions are not minuted, money is mixed, and the settlor carries on as if nothing changed. The control is a trustee who acts like one from the first day, with a written record of every decision, separate accounts, and a calendar of annual reviews.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is naming the closest family member as trustee without asking whether that person has the time, the skill and the independence for a job that may last 30 years and carries personal liability. The second mistake is naming only one trustee with no replacement mechanism. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer who practises trust law in the governing jurisdiction.

Callback

In the asset protection week, Omar and I taught that timing and intent decide whether a transfer survives a creditor's challenge. A trust is one of the vehicles that transfer can go into, which means the same rule applies: a trust set up in calm water, for real family purposes, with a genuine trustee, stands very differently from one set up the week a claim arrives.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. A trust may be taxed separately, or its income may be taxed in the hands of beneficiaries or the settlor; which applies depends entirely on local rules. Liability. The trustee carries personal liability for breach of duty, and may carry liability on contracts signed as trustee unless the contract limits it. Banking. Lenders want to see the deed, the trustees' powers and who must sign. Governance. The deed is the constitution; minutes of decisions are the record. Estate. Property properly held in trust usually sits outside the settlor's own estate, subject to local rules. Exit. Know how the trust ends, who receives what, and what a distribution triggers before you start.

Recap

A trust splits legal title from benefit. The settlor creates it, the trustee holds and manages, the beneficiaries benefit, and the trustee's duties are what make it work. A label is not a trust; behaviour is.

Next lesson: Ford, with Cole assisting, on a trustee who invested trust money in his own deal.
checklist: I can name the settlor, trustee and beneficiaries of any trust I deal with.
I ask to see the trust deed and the trustees' powers before buying from, lending to or partnering with a trust.
I confirm every trustee who must sign has signed, and any required consent is in writing.
I choose trustees for competence, independence and continuity, not closeness.
I make sure every trust has a mechanism to replace a trustee.
I treat any trust I serve on as a set of personal duties, not a formality.
I keep trust money in separate accounts and minute every discretionary decision.
I have a trust lawyer in the governing jurisdiction review any trust before it is signed.
head: Field checklist
speak: A trust is a relationship, not a thing. A settlor hands property to a trustee, who holds the legal title but must use it entirely for the beneficiaries. In most common law systems the trust is not a separate person, so you deal with the trustees and must see that they have power under the deed and that everyone required has signed. A trust is also not a way to keep control while pretending to give it up; if the settlor still decides everything, a court or tax authority may treat the property as still his. What makes a trust valuable is the trustee's duties: honesty, loyalty, following the deed, keeping property separate, keeping records and investing prudently. So choose a trustee for competence, independence and continuity, not affection, and run the trust like a business from day one: written policy, two signatures, annual review and minutes. The law differs by jurisdiction, so a trust lawyer must review any real trust.
terms: Settlor — the person who creates a trust by transferring property to a trustee on stated terms.
Trustee — the person who holds legal title to trust property and must manage it for the beneficiaries under enforceable duties.
Beneficiary — a person for whose benefit trust property is held, with rights against the trustee that depend on the deed.

hostile.q: You say this land is owned by the family trust. Why should I accept the signature of one trustee on the sale agreement?
hostile.a: You should not until you have checked it. I will give you the trust deed, the current list of trustees and the clause that sets out the power to sell and how many trustees must sign. If the deed requires two signatures or a protector's consent, you will get both in writing before closing, and our lawyer will give your lawyer a letter confirming the trustees' authority.

title: The Trustee Who Invested in His Own Deal
summary: A composite case: a family friend serving as trustee lent trust money to his own development company, told himself it was a good investment, and lost most of it. Seven forensic steps show how loyalty, records and independence each failed. The rule that comes out of it is about conflicts, not returns.
body:
This is a composite example. A trustee lent trust money to a company he controlled, the project failed, and the beneficiaries sued him personally; the investment's merits never mattered, because the conflict alone was the breach.

Recall

Q. What does ring-fencing mean in asset protection?

A. Keeping separate risks in separate legal vehicles so a loss in one cannot reach the assets of another, for example one company per project. It works only if the separation is real in money, records and decisions.

Q. What does disability insurance replace?

A. Earned income lost when a person cannot work because of illness or injury. Definitions of disability, waiting periods and benefit periods vary by policy, and a licensed adviser is required before you buy.

Q. What is a privilege log?

A. A list of documents withheld from disclosure because they are privileged, with enough description for the other side to test the claim without seeing the content.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole sits with me today because this failure is a governance and integrity failure that ended in a personal lawsuit. You are a developer. At some point a family, a friend or an investor may ask you to be a trustee, or a trust may be offered as a source of capital for your project. This case teaches you why either situation needs a wall between your two roles. The facts are a composite, assembled from patterns that recur in trust disputes. The numbers are hypothetical round figures, and how a court would decide such a case depends on local law.

1. Timeline

A settlor dies, leaving a trust of 3,000,000 dollars for her three grandchildren, the eldest 12. Her will names a long-time family friend, a local developer, as sole trustee. For three years he invests conservatively and keeps good records. In year four, his own development company needs 1,500,000 dollars of bridge money for a land assembly. Banks want more equity. He lends 1,500,000 dollars from the trust to his company at 10 percent interest, secured by a second mortgage behind the bank. He tells nobody; the beneficiaries are minors and their parents do not read the annual statement closely. In year six the market softens, the bank enforces, and the second mortgage recovers 300,000 dollars. The beneficiaries' parents notice the loss, take legal advice, and sue the trustee personally for 1,200,000 dollars plus the interest the trust would have earned elsewhere.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Accepting a sole trusteeship with no co-trustee and no protector. Deciding to lend trust money to a company he controlled. And deciding not to disclose the loan or seek consent or court approval. Each decision felt reasonable to him. The loan paid 10 percent, more than the trust's bonds. He knew the project. He meant to pay it back.

3. Assumptions

He assumed a good rate made it a good investment. He assumed his knowledge of the project reduced the risk. He assumed that because he intended to repay, there was no conflict. And he assumed nobody would look. Every one of those assumptions turns the duty of loyalty upside down. The question a trust court asks is not whether the investment was good; it is whether the trustee placed himself in a position where his own interest could conflict with his duty.

4. Incentives

The trustee's company needed cheap, patient money that would not demand control. The trust was exactly that, and it answered to him. The beneficiaries were children with no voice. The parents trusted the family friend. Nobody in the arrangement had an incentive or the information to say no, which is precisely the condition in which trustee self-dealing happens.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

There were four. Half the trust's value went into one loan, ignoring any principle of diversification. The security was a second mortgage behind a bank, so the trust took equity-like risk for a debt-like return. The trustee wrote no memorandum explaining why the loan suited the beneficiaries. And the annual statement described the asset as "secured mortgage investment" without naming the borrower, which is how a conflict hides in plain sight. Cole's point is that the last one is the tell: when a document becomes vague exactly where the conflict sits, the author knew.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the day the money left the trust account. Before that, the trustee could have resigned, disclosed, sought consent from adult representatives, or applied to court. After it, every later step was damage control. The bank's enforcement two years later only revealed what the loan decision had already made true.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the market. Markets soften. The root cause was a single trustee with no independent check, holding money he could direct into his own business. The structure invited the conflict, and the trustee accepted the invitation. In many common law systems a trustee who profits from, or deals with, trust property in his own interest without authorisation can be required to restore the loss and give up any gain, regardless of good faith. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it in any jurisdiction.

Cole's angle: the audit trail

An auditor reading this trust's file would ask three questions. Who approved the loan, and where is the record? Was the borrower related to the trustee, and was that disclosed? How did this asset compare with the investment policy? Here, there was no approval, no disclosure and no policy. A second worked example makes the cost concrete, hypothetically. Had the 1,500,000 dollars stayed in a balanced portfolio earning, say, 5 percent a year for two years, it would have grown to roughly 1,654,000 dollars. The trust recovered 300,000 dollars. The claim against the trustee is roughly the difference, about 1,354,000 dollars, before legal costs. A personal claim of that size can consume a developer's own equity.

What a sound process would have looked like

Run the same facts again with a working structure. The deed names two trustees: the family friend and a professional trust company. The investment policy limits any single private investment to 10 percent of the fund and bars loans to any party connected to a trustee without written consent from adult beneficiaries or their representatives, or approval from the court. When the friend's company needs bridge money, he declares the conflict at the trustees' meeting, the minute records it, and he leaves the room. The professional trustee asks two questions: does this loan fit the policy, and would we make it to a stranger on these terms? The answer to both is no, because the loan would be half the fund on second-ranking security. The trust declines. The friend's company finds other money or does not proceed. Nobody sues anybody. Cole's summary is that the cost of the right structure was one co-trustee's fee and one uncomfortable meeting, against a 1,354,000 dollar claim and a broken family friendship. Controls feel expensive only until you price the failure they prevent.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a trustee who is also a businessman will see the trust as available capital. The control is structural: a co-trustee or independent trustee, a written investment policy that forbids related-party transactions without written consent or court approval, and an annual report that names every counterparty.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is believing that a good outcome would have excused the conflict. It usually would not. A trustee who self-deals and wins may still have to give up the profit. The duty is to avoid the conflict, not to win the bet. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer who practises trust law in the governing jurisdiction.

Callback

In the post-mortem on partnerships we took apart a finance chief who sat on both sides of transactions, and Rule 75 said nobody may do that without disclosure, independent pricing and approval by someone with no interest. A trustee lending to his own company is the same failure in a family setting, with weaker supervision and more vulnerable victims.

Recap

A sole trustee lent half a trust to his own company, without disclosure, on second-ranking security, and lost most of it. The market was the trigger; the conflict was the cause.

Rule 90: Never let a trustee deal with trust property for his own benefit or with any party he is connected to unless the deed expressly allows it, every beneficiary or the court has consented in writing, and the decision and its price are documented by someone independent.

Next lesson: Warrick, on what a trust actually costs and returns.
checklist: I refuse any trusteeship where I could be tempted to use the trust as capital for my own business.
I insist on a co-trustee or independent trustee where the trust is large or long.
I require a written investment policy that bars related-party transactions without consent or court approval.
I check that every trust investment names its counterparty in the annual report.
I treat vague wording in a trust statement as a warning sign.
I would resign, disclose or seek approval before a conflicted transaction, never after.
I never take investment from a trust whose trustee is connected to me without independent advice on both sides.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A family friend, also a developer, was sole trustee of a 3,000,000 dollar trust for three grandchildren. In year four his own company needed bridge money, so he lent it 1,500,000 dollars from the trust at 10 percent, on a second mortgage, and told nobody. Two years later the bank enforced and the trust recovered 300,000 dollars. The beneficiaries sued him personally. The investment's merits were irrelevant; the breach was putting himself where his interest conflicted with his duty. The warning signs were concentration, second-ranking security, no written rationale, and a statement that went vague exactly where the borrower should have been named. The root cause was structure: one trustee, no independent check, money he could direct to himself. Rule 90: never let a trustee deal with trust property for his own benefit or a connected party without express power, written consent or court approval, and independent documentation.
terms: Self-dealing — a trustee transacting with trust property in his own interest or with a party connected to him.
Duty of loyalty — a trustee's obligation to act solely for the beneficiaries and never put his own interest in conflict with that duty.
Protector — a person named in some trust deeds with power to approve or veto key trustee decisions, such as replacing a trustee.

hostile.q: You are the trustee of a family trust and you want it to invest in your project. Why is that not a conflict?
hostile.a: It is a conflict, and I will not do it on my own judgment. Either the trust does not invest, or I step aside from that decision entirely: an independent co-trustee decides, with separate legal advice for the trust, a price benchmarked against arm's length terms, written consent from the beneficiaries or approval from the court as the deed and local law require, and full disclosure in the trust's records.

rule: Rule 90: Never let a trustee deal with trust property for his own benefit or with any party he is connected to unless the deed expressly allows it, every beneficiary or the court has consented in writing, and the decision and its price are documented by someone independent.

title: What a Trust Costs and What It Returns
summary: A trust has setup costs, running costs and a drag on returns from fees and taxes. Against those costs sit benefits that are mostly about control, continuity and protection rather than higher returns. Learn to weigh the two in numbers before anyone tells you a trust is free.
body:
A trust rarely raises investment returns; it usually lowers them a little through fees and administration. You pay that cost to buy control, continuity and protection, so the question is always whether what you are buying is worth the drag.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between ring-fencing and hiding assets?

A. Ring-fencing separates risks openly, in advance, for business reasons, and survives scrutiny. Hiding assets moves them to defeat a creditor, and is what voidable transfer rules exist to reverse.

Q. What is the difference between term life and permanent life insurance, in concept?

A. Term insurance covers a fixed period and pays only on death within it. Permanent insurance is designed to last for life and usually builds a cash value, at a higher premium. A licensed adviser is required before you buy.

Q. What is a retention schedule?

A. A written rule for how long each type of record is kept and when and how it is destroyed, set by law, contract and business need.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, people sell trusts with the word "protection" and almost never with a number. A wealth builder thinks in after-cost terms. If a structure costs 1 percent a year of the assets it holds, over 30 years that is a large share of the family's wealth. You need to be able to say, in round numbers, what the trust costs, what it does, and whether a simpler tool, such as a well-drafted will or a corporate holding structure, would do most of the job for less. Everything below is conceptual. Fees and taxes vary widely, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The three layers of cost

Plain English: a trust costs money three ways. It costs something to set up, it costs something every year to run, and it may cost something when it ends or when assets go in and out.

Setup cost is mostly legal: drafting the deed, advice on tax and on how the assets get into the trust, and possibly a valuation. Transferring assets in can itself be a taxable event in some systems, which is often the largest setup cost and the one people forget. Running cost has two parts. The first is a trustee fee: what a professional trustee charges, often a percentage of assets, a fixed fee, or both. The second is administration: accounting, tax filings, audits, investment management and legal reviews. Ending cost includes distributions that may trigger tax, final accounts and legal work.

Applied example, hypothetical round numbers. A family puts 5,000,000 dollars of investments into a trust. Setup costs 40,000 dollars. A professional trustee charges 0.5 percent a year, which is 25,000 dollars. Accounting and filings cost 10,000 dollars a year. Investment management costs a further 0.6 percent, 30,000 dollars, though that would be paid with or without a trust. The cost that exists only because of the trust is about 35,000 dollars a year, or 0.7 percent of the assets.

Drag over time

The professional framing is cost drag: the difference between the return the assets earn and the return the beneficiaries actually receive. A small annual drag compounds into a large number.

Second worked example. Suppose the 5,000,000 dollars earns 6 percent a year before trust costs. Over 25 years without the trust-only costs, it grows by a factor of about 4.29, to roughly 21,460,000 dollars. With a 0.7 percent drag, the net return is 5.3 percent, a factor of about 3.64, giving roughly 18,180,000 dollars. The drag costs the family about 3,280,000 dollars over 25 years. That is the price of the trust's benefits, stated in the only unit that matters.

Say that out loud now.

What the cost buys

Against that price, a trust can buy several things, and each has a value you can at least estimate. Continuity: the assets do not freeze when a parent dies or loses capacity, because the trustee keeps managing. Control over timing: a 19-year-old does not receive a lump sum outright. Protection: in some circumstances, property held by a properly constituted trust may be harder for a beneficiary's creditor or former spouse to reach, depending on local law. Privacy, in some systems, compared with a public probate file. And tax effects, which may be positive, neutral or negative depending entirely on the rules.

The discipline is to put a rough value on each. If the main goal is to stop an 18-year-old receiving 5,000,000 dollars outright, the value is large and the 0.7 percent drag looks cheap. If the main goal is vague "protection" for an adult who has no creditors and no marital risk, a simpler structure may deliver most of the benefit for a fraction of the cost.

The developer's version

For a developer, the asset in trust is often not a portfolio but shares in a holding company that owns projects. That changes the costs. The trustee must understand a private business, receive company accounts, and make decisions about dividends and reinvestment. Professional trustees charge more for that, and some will not do it. It also changes the risk: a trustee holding a concentrated private stake may need explicit permission in the deed to hold it without diversifying, or he may face a claim for failing to diversify. You saw in the capital allocation week that concentration is a deliberate risk; inside a trust, it must be a written one.

Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, assets you have genuinely transferred into a trust you do not control are no longer yours. They leave your net worth and enter the family's. That improves protection and estate position, and it reduces your personal liquidity and your borrowing base. Lenders who once counted those assets toward your guarantee strength will not count them now. Before you settle a trust, recompute your liquidity floor and guarantee capacity without those assets.

Working with advisers

Ask every adviser proposing a trust for a one-page cost table: setup, annual, and exit, in dollars, and the drag over 20 years. An adviser who will not put the cost in writing is selling, not advising. Ask too who earns what if you say yes; trust companies, lawyers and investment managers may each be paid differently.

And ask the adviser what the simpler alternative would cost and achieve. A good adviser will tell you when you do not need the trust.

When a trust is the wrong tool

Some goals do not need a trust at all. If the aim is simply that assets pass to an adult spouse at death, a well-drafted will and correctly named beneficiaries on accounts may do it at a fraction of the cost. If the aim is to separate business risk, a corporate structure does that job, and a trust adds nothing. If the aim is to save tax, be careful: tax rules on trusts change, and a structure built for one rule can become a cost centre when the rule moves. A useful test is to write the trust's purpose in one sentence a teenager would understand. "To hold the family company shares until the youngest child is 30, so no child can sell or borrow against them before then" is a purpose. "Asset protection and tax efficiency" is a brochure. If you cannot write the sentence, you are not yet ready to pay for the structure, and an adviser should help you write it before anyone drafts a deed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is buying a trust for an unpriced benefit while paying a priced cost for decades. The control is a written cost-and-benefit page before signing, reviewed every few years, with a plan to wind the trust up if it no longer earns its keep, where the deed and local law allow.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is ignoring the cost of getting assets into the trust. In some systems, transferring an appreciated asset is treated as a sale, and the tax due on day one can dwarf every annual fee. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Callback

In the beyond-real-estate week we said fees are certain and returns are not, so a fee is a guaranteed loss you must justify. Trust costs are the same kind of number. Compound them, then decide.

Recap

A trust costs money to set up, run and end. A small annual drag compounds into millions over a generation. Price the benefits, compare a simpler tool, and recompute your own balance sheet without the transferred assets.

Next lesson: Tessa, on the rules: discretionary and fixed trusts, and the trustee's legal duties.
checklist: I ask for setup, annual and exit costs in dollars before any trust is signed.
I compute the cost drag over at least 20 years.
I price the main benefit the trust buys and compare it with a simpler tool.
I check whether transferring assets in is itself a taxable event.
I confirm the deed allows the trustee to hold a concentrated private stake if that is the asset.
I recompute my liquidity floor and guarantee capacity without the transferred assets.
I ask every adviser how they are paid if I proceed.
I review whether the trust still earns its cost every few years.

speak: A trust rarely raises returns; it lowers them a little through fees and administration, and you pay that to buy control, continuity and protection. Cost comes in three layers: setup, running and exit. Hypothetically, a 5,000,000 dollar trust might carry about 35,000 dollars a year of trust-only cost, 0.7 percent. At 6 percent gross over 25 years, that drag costs about 3,280,000 dollars. That is the price, so put a value on what it buys: continuity at death or incapacity, control over when beneficiaries receive money, possible protection, privacy, and tax effects that may help or hurt. Watch the cost of getting assets in, which in some systems is treated as a sale. On your own balance sheet, assets truly in trust are no longer yours, so your liquidity and guarantee capacity fall. Ask every adviser for a written cost table and the simpler alternative. A licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Trustee fee — what a trustee charges to administer a trust, often a percentage of assets, a fixed fee, or both.
Cost drag — the gap between the return assets earn and the return beneficiaries receive after fees and costs.
Liquidity floor — the minimum readily available cash a person keeps to meet obligations without forced sales.

hostile.q: You transferred your holding company shares into a family trust last year. Why should I still count them in your net worth for this guarantee?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. Those shares are held by independent trustees for my children and I do not control them. My statement of net worth shows only what I own personally, and I have recomputed my liquid assets and contingent liabilities without the trust. If that is not enough for the guarantee you want, we should talk about a lower cap or a different form of credit support.

title: Discretionary or Fixed, and the Duties That Bind the Trustee
summary: A fixed trust gives each beneficiary a defined share; a discretionary trust lets the trustee decide who gets what. Both are governed by the deed and by a core of trustee duties that the law imposes whatever the deed says. Learn the two types, the duties, and the documents a careful trustee keeps.
body:
The trust deed says what the trustee may do; the law says how he must do it. A fixed trust leaves the trustee little to decide, a discretionary trust leaves him a great deal, and the more he can decide, the more his duties matter.

Recall

Q. Who holds legal title to trust property?

A. The trustee. The beneficiaries hold the benefit, and the trustee must use the property entirely for them under the deed.

Q. In concept, why does a court look at timing in an asset protection challenge?

A. Because a transfer made when no claim was in view looks like planning, while one made after a claim appeared looks like an attempt to defeat a creditor. The tests and periods differ by jurisdiction.

Q. What does a lender's monitor or quantity surveyor audit add to an owner's own reporting?

A. An independent check by someone with no stake in the result, which catches optimism and errors the owner's own team will not see.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you read a trust deed, whether as a prospective trustee, a buyer, a lender or a family member, you are reading two things at once: the powers the settlor granted and the duties the law adds on top. You need both to judge whether a trustee's decision is valid. This is concept teaching. Trust law differs by jurisdiction, and a trust lawyer in the governing jurisdiction must advise on any real trust.

Fixed and discretionary

Plain English. In a fixed trust, the deed sets each beneficiary's share. "Income to my spouse for life, then capital to my two children equally" is fixed: the trustee administers, but does not choose who benefits. In a discretionary trust, the deed names a class of possible beneficiaries and lets the trustee decide whether, when and how much each receives. "The trustees may pay income or capital to any of my descendants, in such shares as they decide" is discretionary.

The professional framing. In a fixed trust, each beneficiary has a defined interest that may be valued, may sometimes be reachable by that beneficiary's creditors, and may be taxable to that beneficiary. In a discretionary trust, a beneficiary typically has only a hope, plus the right to be considered and to have the trust properly administered. That difference is why discretionary trusts are often used for flexibility and, in some systems, for protection. It is also why they demand more of the trustee: every discretionary decision is a judgment that must be made properly.

Applied example, hypothetical. A discretionary trust holds 2,000,000 dollars for a settlor's four grandchildren. One grandchild wants 200,000 dollars to start a business. The trustee must consider the request, look at that grandchild's needs and the others' interests, consider the settlor's wishes, take advice if needed, decide, and record the reasons. If he simply says yes because the grandchild is persuasive, or no because he dislikes the idea, without real consideration, the decision may be open to challenge.

Say that out loud now.

The core duties

Whatever the deed says, common law systems generally impose a core of duties on trustees. Concepts only; verify each against the primary source in the governing jurisdiction before you rely on it.

  • Follow the terms. The trustee must act within the deed. A payment the deed does not authorise is a breach, however well meant.
  • Loyalty. No conflict between personal interest and duty, no unauthorised profit, no dealing with trust property for himself. Rule 90 came from this duty.
  • Prudence in investment. Many systems require the trustee to invest as a prudent person would, usually with attention to diversification and to the beneficiaries' needs, unless the deed permits otherwise.
  • Impartiality. Balance the interests of different beneficiaries, for example an income beneficiary today and capital beneficiaries later.
  • Keep property separate and account. Hold trust assets apart from the trustee's own, keep records, and provide information to beneficiaries as the law requires.
  • Act personally and jointly. Trustees usually cannot hand their discretion to someone else, though they may delegate administration and investment management with care; where there are several trustees, they generally act together.

The documents that sit around the deed

A well-run trust has more than a deed. A letter of wishes is a non-binding note from the settlor explaining what she hopes the trustees will consider, for example "help with education first, then housing". It guides discretion without fettering it. A minutes book records every decision. An investment policy sets risk and asset limits. A register lists trust assets and where they are held. And an annual account shows what came in, what went out, and why.

Second applied example, hypothetical. A developer is asked to buy a parcel from a discretionary family trust for 4,000,000 dollars. His lawyer asks for four things: the deed, to confirm a power of sale; the current trustee appointments, to confirm who must sign; any consent the deed requires, such as a protector's; and a trustees' resolution approving the sale at that price, ideally with a valuation. If the trustees sell below value to a friend, the beneficiaries may challenge it, and a buyer who knew of the problem may be exposed too. The resolution and valuation protect both sides.

Liability, exoneration and indemnity

A trustee who breaches a duty can be personally liable to restore the loss. Some deeds contain an exoneration clause limiting a trustee's liability for honest mistakes. How far such clauses work, and whether they can ever excuse dishonesty or gross negligence, depends on local law. Trustees are also usually entitled to be reimbursed from the trust for properly incurred expenses, but not for costs of their own breach. If you are asked to serve as a trustee, read the exoneration and indemnity clauses before you agree, and consider whether you need your own insurance or legal advice.

How long a trust may last, and how it may change

Many common law systems limit how long property can be tied up in a trust, through a rule against perpetuities or a statutory maximum period, and some have relaxed or abolished the limit. Some tax systems also impose their own clock on trusts, which you will meet next week. Verify the period and its effect against the primary source in the governing jurisdiction before you rely on it. For a developer the practical point is that a trust holding project company shares may have to distribute or restructure at a date set decades earlier, and that date may fall in the middle of a development cycle. Read the trust's end date and vesting provisions the way you read a loan maturity. A related concept is variation: whether the trustees, a protector, the beneficiaries together or a court can change the trust's terms. Some deeds give wide powers to amend; others give almost none. A trust that cannot adapt to a changed family or a changed law can become a trap. Ask, before signing, what changes are possible and who must agree.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in a discretionary trust is a decision made without process: no consideration of the class, no reasons, no record. The control is a standard decision memo for every distribution: the request, the beneficiary's circumstances, the effect on others, the settlor's wishes, the advice taken, the decision and the reasons.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is treating the letter of wishes as binding instructions, or ignoring it altogether. It is neither. It is evidence of the settlor's purpose that a trustee should weigh, while keeping his own judgment. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer who practises trust law in the governing jurisdiction.

Callback

In the records week, Vera taught that a contemporaneous record is evidence and a later recollection is argument. A trustee's minutes book is exactly that: the evidence, made at the time, that each discretionary decision was considered properly. Without it, a trustee defends himself from memory.

Recap

Fixed trusts set shares; discretionary trusts give the trustee judgment. Either way the trustee must follow the deed, be loyal, invest prudently, be impartial, keep property separate, account and act personally. The letter of wishes guides; the minutes prove.

Next lesson: Nadia, reverse engineering how much a trust needs to hold to fund a promised distribution.
checklist: I can tell whether a trust is fixed or discretionary from its deed.
I check the deed for powers of sale, investment and distribution before relying on any trustee decision.
I ask for a trustees' resolution and a valuation when buying from a trust.
I confirm any required protector or beneficiary consent is in writing.
I treat a letter of wishes as guidance, not instruction.
I use a written decision memo for every discretionary distribution.
I read exoneration and indemnity clauses before agreeing to serve as trustee.
I keep trust assets in a register, separate from my own.
head: Field checklist
speak: The deed says what a trustee may do; the law says how he must do it. In a fixed trust, the deed sets each beneficiary's share. In a discretionary trust, the trustee decides who in a class receives what and when, so beneficiaries often hold only a hope and a right to proper administration. That flexibility is why discretionary trusts demand more of the trustee. In common law systems the core duties are: follow the terms, be loyal and avoid conflicts, invest prudently, treat beneficiaries impartially, keep property separate and account, and act personally and jointly. Around the deed sit a letter of wishes, which guides but does not bind, a minutes book, an investment policy, an asset register and annual accounts. When you buy from a trust, see the deed, the trustees, any required consent, a resolution and a valuation. Rules vary by jurisdiction, so a trust lawyer must advise.
terms: Fixed trust — a trust whose deed sets each beneficiary's share, leaving the trustee no choice about who benefits.
Discretionary trust — a trust whose deed lets the trustee decide which members of a class receive income or capital, when and in what amounts.
Letter of wishes — a non-binding note from a settlor explaining what she hopes trustees will consider when exercising discretion.

hostile.q: The trustees approved a 300,000 dollar distribution to one grandchild and nothing to the other three. How do I know that was a proper decision and not favouritism?
hostile.a: Read the minute. It records the request, each beneficiary's circumstances, the settlor's letter of wishes, the effect on the remaining fund and the reasons for the decision, with the advice the trustees took. If the minute does not show real consideration of all four, you have grounds to ask the trustees to explain, and our lawyer can advise on your rights as a beneficiary.

title: Reverse Engineering the Fund a Promise Requires
summary: Start from a promised outcome, such as a fixed yearly payment to a beneficiary, and work backward to the trust fund needed to support it after fees, tax and inflation. The method exposes how much capital a simple promise really consumes. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
A promise of a yearly payment from a trust has a price in capital, and you can find it by working backward: from the payment, through inflation, fees and tax, to the fund that can keep the promise without running dry.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a fixed and a discretionary trust?

A. A fixed trust sets each beneficiary's share in the deed. A discretionary trust lets the trustee decide who in a class receives what, when and how much.

Q. How do you size life insurance needs from first principles?

A. Add debts to clear, future obligations to fund and income to replace, subtract assets that would be available, and the gap is the need. A licensed adviser is required before you buy.

Q. What does document control mean on a project?

A. A system that ensures everyone works from the current version of each document, with a log of revisions, issues and approvals.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, families make promises through trusts: "the trust will pay my mother 60,000 dollars a year for life", or "each grandchild will receive help with university". A trustee then has to keep that promise with real money, net of costs, for years. If nobody worked backward from the promise to the capital it needs, the trustee will one day face a choice between breaking the promise and draining the fund. This lesson is a method, not a forecast. All numbers are hypothetical round figures, chosen for clean arithmetic; real returns, fees, tax and inflation are uncertain, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The finished outcome

Start with the outcome. A trust must pay a beneficiary 60,000 dollars a year in today's money, rising with inflation, for 25 years. At the end, the fund may be fully spent. The question is: how large must the fund be on day one?

We work backward through four layers: inflation, the trust's after-cost return, tax on that return, and the payment period.

Step one: the net return the fund must earn

Assume, hypothetically, that the portfolio earns 6.0 percent a year before costs. Trustee and administration fees cost 0.8 percent a year. That leaves 5.2 percent. Assume tax inside the trust takes one quarter of the return, a hypothetical figure only; real trust taxation depends entirely on the jurisdiction and the type of income, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. One quarter of 5.2 percent is 1.3 percent, leaving 3.9 percent after fees and tax.

Now inflation. If prices rise 2.5 percent a year and the payment must keep pace, the fund's real return, the return above inflation, is roughly 3.9 minus 2.5, about 1.4 percent. The precise figure is (1.039 divided by 1.025) minus 1, which is about 1.37 percent. Working in real terms lets us keep the payment flat at 60,000 dollars of today's money.

Say that out loud now.

Step two: the fund the payment requires

The fund needed is the present value of an annuity: the lump sum today that, earning a given return, pays a fixed amount each year for a set number of years and is then exhausted. The formula, in words: payment multiplied by one minus one over one-plus-the-rate raised to the number of years, all divided by the rate.

At a real rate of 1.37 percent over 25 years, one-plus-the-rate raised to 25 is about 1.405. One over that is about 0.712. One minus 0.712 is 0.288. Divided by 0.0137, that gives an annuity factor of about 21.0. Multiply by 60,000 dollars and the required fund is about 1,260,000 dollars.

Check it against intuition. Twenty-five payments of 60,000 dollars total 1,500,000 dollars in today's money. A fund of 1,260,000 dollars covers it only because it keeps earning a small real return. If the real return were zero, you would need the full 1,500,000 dollars.

Step three: what each assumption is worth

Reverse engineering is most useful when you change one assumption at a time and watch the answer move. Second worked example: suppose fees are 1.5 percent instead of 0.8. The pre-tax net return falls to 4.5 percent, after tax 3.375 percent, real return about 0.85 percent. The annuity factor rises to about 22.5, and the required fund to about 1,350,000 dollars. Seven-tenths of a percent of extra fees adds about 90,000 dollars to the capital the promise needs on day one.

Now suppose the beneficiary lives longer and the promise runs 35 years instead of 25, at the original 1.37 percent real return. One-plus-the-rate raised to 35 is about 1.61; one over that is 0.621; one minus that is 0.379; divided by 0.0137, the factor is about 27.7. The required fund rises to about 1,660,000 dollars. A promise "for life" is a promise with an unknown end date, and that uncertainty is expensive.

CaseReal returnYearsFund needed
Base1.37 percent25about 1,260,000 dollars
Higher fees0.85 percent25about 1,350,000 dollars
Longer life1.37 percent35about 1,660,000 dollars

Step four: protect the promise

A trustee cannot control markets, but can control how the promise is written and funded. Three controls follow from the numbers. Fund for the long case, not the base case, if the promise is for life. Write the promise with some flexibility, for example "up to" an amount, or "as the trustees consider appropriate", if the settlor's real goal allows. And review the fund against the promise every year, recomputing the factor with actual returns, so a shortfall is seen in year three rather than year twenty.

Step five: the same method for a capital promise

Not every promise is a stream. Some are lump sums at a future date, such as "the trust will provide 100,000 dollars to each of my four grandchildren when they turn 18". Suppose, hypothetically, the grandchildren turn 18 in 5, 8, 11 and 14 years, and the promise is in today's money. Use the same real return of 1.37 percent. The present value of each lump sum is 100,000 dollars divided by one-plus-the-rate raised to the number of years. For 5 years, 1.0137 to the 5th is about 1.070, giving about 93,500 dollars. For 8 years, about 1.115, giving about 89,700 dollars. For 11 years, about 1.162, giving about 86,100 dollars. For 14 years, about 1.210, giving about 82,600 dollars. The total fund needed today is about 351,900 dollars, against a face value of 400,000 dollars. The pattern to notice is that distant promises are cheaper to fund today, but only if the trust really earns the assumed real return for the whole period. A shortfall in returns hits the last grandchild hardest, which is a fairness problem as well as a funding one.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a fixed promise funded on optimistic assumptions. The fund runs short late, when the beneficiary is oldest and most dependent. The control is an annual sustainability test: current fund divided by the annuity factor for the remaining years at a conservative real return. If that figure falls below the promised payment, the trustees act now.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is working in nominal numbers and forgetting inflation. A flat 60,000 dollars a year that does not rise loses about a third of its buying power over 16 years at 2.5 percent inflation. Decide whether the promise is nominal or real, and model it the same way.

Callback

In the time value of money week, Nadia taught that a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now, and net present value is how you compare them. This lesson is that same idea used backward: the trust's promise is a stream of future dollars, and the fund is its present value after costs.

Recap

Start from the promise. Strip fees, tax and inflation to get a real net return. Use the annuity factor to find the fund. Then test fees and longevity, fund for the long case, and review every year.

Next lesson: Tessa, in the room with a family choosing a trustee.
checklist: I start from the promised payment and its duration before discussing the fund.
I decide whether the promise is nominal or real and model it consistently.
I deduct fees and tax before applying inflation.
I compute the annuity factor and the required fund.
I test higher fees and longer duration, one at a time.
I fund a lifetime promise on the long case, not the base case.
I run an annual sustainability test against the remaining promise.
I have a licensed adviser review the assumptions before the trust is funded.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every trust promise has a price in capital, and you find it by working backward. Hypothetically, a trust must pay 60,000 dollars a year in today's money for 25 years. Start with a 6 percent gross return, subtract 0.8 percent of fees to get 5.2, take a hypothetical quarter for tax to get 3.9, then remove 2.5 percent inflation for a real return of about 1.37 percent. The annuity factor at that rate over 25 years is about 21, so the fund needed is about 1,260,000 dollars. Raise fees to 1.5 percent and the fund rises to about 1,350,000. Stretch the promise to 35 years and it rises to about 1,660,000. So fund a lifetime promise for the long case, write flexibility into the promise where the settlor's goal allows, and test sustainability every year. Real returns, fees and tax are uncertain, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Present value of an annuity — the lump sum today that, earning a given return, pays a fixed amount each year for a set period and is then exhausted.
Real return — the return on an investment after removing the effect of inflation.
Sustainability test — a periodic check of whether a fund can still meet its remaining promised payments under conservative assumptions.

hostile.q: The settlor promised my client 60,000 dollars a year for life. Why are the trustees now saying the fund may not last?
hostile.a: Because we tested it. On current returns, fees and a conservative life expectancy, the fund supports about 52,000 dollars a year in real terms for the full period, not 60,000. We are telling you in year three, not year twenty. We can show you the calculation, and the options are to reduce the payment a little now, add capital, or accept a higher risk of a shortfall later. We want your client's view before we decide.

title: The Family That Wants a Trustee They Can Control
summary: A realistic scene: a hypothetical family asks Mr Shabazz to serve as trustee and quietly expects him to do what one of them says. Learn the lines that set the duty first, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and when to decline.
body:
When someone asks you to be a trustee, they are often asking you to be their ally. Your job in that room is to make clear, kindly and early, that a trustee's loyalty belongs to all the beneficiaries and to the deed, not to the person asking.

Recall

Q. What does the duty of impartiality require?

A. That the trustee balance the interests of different beneficiaries, for example someone receiving income today and those receiving capital later, rather than favour one.

Q. What is key-person risk in a developer's business?

A. The risk that the business loses much of its value or capacity if one person, often the founder, dies, is disabled or leaves.

Q. Why should project correspondence be filed by a system rather than in personal inboxes?

A. So that the organisation, not one person's memory, holds the record, and so that it can be found and produced when a dispute arises.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as your reputation grows, people will ask you to be a trustee because you are capable and trusted. That request is a compliment and a risk. The scene below is hypothetical. The family, the numbers and the trust are invented for teaching. What is real is the pattern: one family member hopes the trustee will be their voice.

The scene

A hypothetical widower in his seventies, whom we will call Mr Allen, plans a discretionary trust of 4,000,000 dollars for his three adult children. His eldest son, Daniel, who works with him in business, arranges a lunch with you. Daniel says: "Dad wants you as one of the trustees. You understand property, and you understand us. My sister has had money problems and my brother lives abroad and does not really care. You and I can just keep things sensible." The father arrives later and confirms he wants you, with Daniel as the other trustee.

The question behind the question

Daniel's real question is: will you vote with me? The father's real question is: will you make sure my children are treated well after I am gone, including the one I worry about? Those two questions are not the same, and a good trustee answers the father's, in front of both.

The lines to say

To Daniel, early and plainly: "I would be honoured to be considered. I should be clear about one thing first. If I am a trustee, my duty is to all three of you equally, and to what your father writes in the deed. I would not be able to agree anything in advance with any one beneficiary."

To the father: "Before I say yes, may I ask what you most want the trust to do? And what you most worry about?" Then listen. He may say his daughter's finances keep him awake at night, or that he fears the children will fall out.

Then: "Those are exactly the things a letter of wishes should record, in your words, so the trustees know your purpose. I would also suggest an independent trustee or a protector alongside the family trustee, so that no decision depends on one relationship."

On practicalities: "I would want to see the draft deed, understand my powers and liability, and know how a trustee is paid and replaced. I would also want our own lawyer to explain my duties to me before I sign."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "Don't worry, Daniel and I will sort things out." That sentence pre-commits your discretion to one beneficiary, which is the opposite of the duty you are taking on, and it will be quoted back to you in any dispute.

Never say anything about another beneficiary's character, such as "Yes, your sister does sound like a problem." A trustee must consider each beneficiary's circumstances fairly when a request comes; forming a view at lunch, before the trust exists, poisons that.

Never say "I'll do it as a favour, no need for fees or paperwork." Unpaid trustees still carry full duties, and paperwork is your protection.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you ask the father what he most wants. Silence gives him room to say the thing he has not said to his children. Stay silent, too, when Daniel pushes back with "Come on, we both know how this works." Let the sentence sit. Then repeat calmly: "I understand. My answer is the same."

Holding your state

Daniel is an important person in your business world, and saying no to him feels costly. Notice the pressure as a fact, not a command. Slow your breathing and your speech. Remind yourself that the most valuable thing you bring to this family is independence, and that independence spent at lunch cannot be bought back later.

When to decline

A worked example of the decision, hypothetical. You weigh three factors. Conflict: you do business with Daniel, which creates a risk you will be seen to favour him; with an independent co-trustee and a written conflicts policy, the risk may be manageable, without one it is not. Capacity: a trust of 4,000,000 dollars with an anxious family may need 30 hours a year of your time for decades. Liability: if the deed has no reasonable exoneration clause and no indemnity, a wrong call could put your own assets at risk. If two of the three factors are against you, decline gracefully: "I care about this family too much to take a role I cannot do well. Let me introduce you to two professional trustees."

How the best do it

Professional trustees typically hold a first meeting with the settlor alone, record his wishes, explain their duties in writing, and decline any request to agree outcomes with a beneficiary in advance. They also refuse appointment where they act for one beneficiary in another matter, unless the conflict is disclosed and managed. A small developer can copy the sequence exactly: meet the settlor alone, write down the purpose, state the duty, and check conflicts before agreeing.

If you accept: the first ninety days

Suppose the deed is sound, an independent trustee is appointed, and you accept. The first ninety days set the habits that protect you for decades. In the first month, take your own legal advice on your duties and read the deed twice, noting every power, consent and deadline. Open trust accounts in the trustees' names, never in yours personally. In the second month, build the asset register, adopt a written investment policy, and agree a conflicts policy that names your business relationship with Daniel and states that you will step out of any decision it touches. In the third month, hold the first formal trustees' meeting, minute it, set a calendar of annual reviews, and write to each beneficiary explaining who the trustees are and how to make a request. Each of those steps is boring. Each is also a piece of evidence that you behaved as a trustee from day one, and evidence is what protects a trustee when a disappointed beneficiary later says otherwise.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting the role on a private understanding with one beneficiary. The control is to state your duty to all beneficiaries before you accept, in front of the settlor, and to insist on an independent trustee or protector where you have a business relationship with any beneficiary.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is saying yes at the lunch table. The right answer to an invitation to be trustee is always "I am honoured; let me see the deed and take advice." Professional sign-off required: a lawyer who practises trust law in the governing jurisdiction.

Callback

In the negotiation week, Kema and JAX taught that every request carries an interest behind the position. Daniel's position is "be my co-trustee"; his interest is influence. The father's position is "be a trustee"; his interest is fairness after his death. Answering the interest is how you serve the right person.

Recap

State the duty first, ask the settlor what he wants and fears, propose independence, read the deed, take advice, and decline when conflict, capacity or liability is against you.

Next lesson: Kema, with six questions and drills on trusts.
checklist: I never say yes to a trusteeship at the first conversation.
I state, before accepting, that my duty is to all beneficiaries and the deed.
I ask the settlor what he most wants and most fears, and suggest he records it in a letter of wishes.
I propose an independent trustee or protector where I have a business tie to a beneficiary.
I read the draft deed, my powers, liability, indemnity and replacement terms.
I take my own legal advice on my duties before signing.
I never comment on one beneficiary's character to another.
I decline when conflict, capacity or liability is against me.
head: Field checklist
speak: When someone asks you to be a trustee, they are often asking you to be their ally. In the hypothetical scene, a business contact, Daniel, says his father wants you as co-trustee and that the two of you can keep things sensible. The question behind his question is whether you will vote with him. The father's question is whether his children will be treated fairly, including the one he worries about. Answer the father's, in front of both: my duty would be to all three children equally and to the deed, and I could not agree anything in advance with any one beneficiary. Ask the father what he most wants and fears, then stay silent. Suggest a letter of wishes and an independent trustee or protector. Never pre-commit your discretion, never comment on another beneficiary, and never skip the paperwork. Read the deed, take advice, and decline if conflict, capacity or liability is against you.
terms: Co-trustee — one of two or more trustees who generally must act together on decisions.
Independent trustee — a trustee with no family or business tie to the beneficiaries, often a professional or trust company.
Conflicts policy — a written rule for how a trustee identifies, discloses and manages situations where personal interests could affect decisions.

hostile.q: You do business with my brother and you are now a trustee of our father's trust. Why should I believe you are not just his vote?
hostile.a: You should not have to take my word for it. The deed appoints an independent trustee alongside us, every distribution decision is minuted with reasons, and I have disclosed my business relationship with your brother in writing and step out of any decision where it is relevant. You are entitled to see the minutes of decisions that affect you, and if you think a decision was not properly made, you can ask us to explain it or take your own legal advice.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 90 Review: Trusts as Relationships and Duties
summary: Six questions test the week on settlors, trustees, beneficiaries, fixed and discretionary trusts, cost drag and trustee duties. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical trustee minute. A boardroom drill explains trusts in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a trust is only as good as the trustee's behaviour, so every question about a trust is really a question about duty, independence and records.

Recall

Q. What is the annuity factor used for in trust planning?

A. To convert a promised yearly payment over a period into the lump-sum fund needed today, at a given after-cost real return.

Q. Why is a fraudulent or voidable transfer challenge about timing?

A. Because transfers made when a claim was known or likely look like an attempt to defeat creditors, and courts and statutes look back over defined periods that vary by jurisdiction.

Q. What should every project record show to be useful later?

A. Who made it, when, what it relates to, and what was decided, so a stranger can understand it years later without the author.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, trusts will reach you as a planner, a counterparty and possibly a trustee. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can read a trust deed with a lawyer and ask the right questions. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the three roles in a trust and what each holds.

Answer: The settlor creates the trust and transfers property. The trustee holds legal title and manages it. The beneficiaries hold the benefit and the right to proper administration.

Question 2. Why is a trust that the settlor fully controls at risk?

Answer: Because a court or tax authority may decide no genuine trust was intended and treat the property as still the settlor's. A label does not change who really owns and controls it.

Question 3. What is the difference between a fixed and a discretionary trust?

Answer: A fixed trust sets each beneficiary's share. A discretionary trust lets the trustee decide who in a class receives what and when, which makes each decision a judgment that must be properly made and recorded.

Question 4. State Rule 90 and the duty it comes from.

Answer: Never let a trustee deal with trust property for his own benefit or with a connected party unless the deed allows it, beneficiaries or the court consent in writing, and the decision and price are documented independently. It comes from the duty of loyalty.

Question 5. What is cost drag, and why does it matter over a generation?

Answer: The gap between what assets earn and what beneficiaries receive after fees and costs. A drag of under 1 percent a year compounds into millions over 25 years, so it must be weighed against the benefits it buys.

Question 6. What should you say when asked to become a trustee?

Answer: That you are honoured, that your duty would be to all beneficiaries and the deed, and that you need to see the deed and take advice before deciding.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Tessa framed a trust as a relationship that splits legal title from benefit. Ford and Cole took apart a composite trustee who lent half a trust to his own company, giving Rule 90. Warrick priced a trust's cost drag and what it buys. Tessa taught fixed and discretionary trusts and the core trustee duties. Nadia reverse engineered the fund a lifetime promise needs. Tessa ran the lunch where a beneficiary tried to recruit the trustee.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical trustees' minute and find the defects before reading on.

Minute of the Trustees of the Hypothetical Family Trust. Present: J. Brown (trustee). The trustee considered a request from the eldest beneficiary for 250,000 dollars to buy a house. The trustee knows the beneficiary well and considers him responsible. The other beneficiaries were not considered as the request came from the eldest. The trustee also approved a loan of 400,000 dollars from the trust to Brown Developments Ltd at 9 percent, which is a better return than the bank. The letter of wishes was not consulted as it is not binding. Approved.

The defects. First, only one trustee is present; if the deed requires two trustees to act jointly, the decisions may be invalid. Second, the distribution was decided on personal familiarity, with no consideration of the other beneficiaries, breaching the duty to consider the class and to be impartial. Third, the loan to Brown Developments Ltd, which appears connected to the trustee, is self-dealing with no disclosure, consent or independent pricing, a breach of Rule 90. Fourth, justifying the loan by its rate repeats the composite case's error: a good return does not cure a conflict. Fifth, ignoring the letter of wishes because it is not binding misunderstands its role; it should be weighed. Sixth, no reasons, advice or effect on the fund are recorded, so the minute cannot defend the decisions.

Common confusions

Four confusions recur, and each is worth saying aloud. First, "the trust signed the contract". In most common law systems the trust is not a person; the trustees signed, and they may carry the obligation personally unless the contract limits it. Second, "it is in trust, so creditors cannot touch it". Whether creditors can reach trust property depends on who settled it, when, why, what interest each beneficiary has, and local law; there is no blanket answer. Third, "I am the beneficiary, so I can tell the trustee what to do". A beneficiary can usually require proper administration and, in some cases, information, but a discretionary beneficiary cannot direct a distribution. Fourth, "the trustee is family, so we do not need records". Family trustees need records more, because family disputes are where trust litigation most often begins. If you hear any of these four sentences in a meeting, slow the conversation down and ask the lawyer in the room to correct it on the record.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is accepting the language of trusts without the behaviour. The control is to test any trust you meet against four questions: who decides, who checks, what is recorded, and what conflicts exist. If any of the four has no clear answer, the trust is not yet safe to rely on, whether you are buying from it, lending to it, investing alongside it or being asked to serve it. Ask for the missing answer in writing, and let the lawyer for the trust provide it before you commit.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is assuming a family trust needs less discipline than a company. It needs more, because its beneficiaries are often less able to protect themselves.

Boardroom drill

Explain trusts in two minutes to a lender who asks why a family trust is on your ownership chart. Then read the model answer.

Model answer: "A trust is a legal relationship, not a company. The trustees hold the shares in their own names, for the benefit of my children, under duties the law enforces. I am not a trustee, and I do not control the shares, which is why they do not appear in my personal net worth. The trustees are an independent professional and a family member, and the deed requires both to sign. The deed allows them to hold this private stake without diversifying, and it bars related-party transactions without written consent. You will get the deed, the trustee appointments and a trustees' resolution for any document they sign. If you need recourse, it comes from me personally, on my own balance sheet, not from the trust."

Callback

In the integrity week, REGA and Cole taught beneficial ownership: who really owns and controls an asset behind the names on the register. A trust is the clearest case. Lenders and authorities will ask who the settlor, trustees and beneficiaries are, and the honest answer must match the deed.

Recap

Trusts split title from benefit, run on duties, cost money, and succeed or fail on independence and records.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, trusts. A trust splits legal title, held by the trustee, from the benefit, held by beneficiaries, and it is only as good as the trustee's behaviour. A settlor who keeps full control risks the trust being treated as a label. Fixed trusts set shares; discretionary trusts give the trustee judgment, so each decision needs consideration of the whole class, impartiality and a written record. Rule 90 says a trustee must never deal with trust property for himself or a connected party without express power, written consent or court approval, and independent documentation; the composite case showed that a good rate does not cure a conflict. A trust's cost drag, even under 1 percent a year, compounds into millions, so price what it buys. A lifetime promise needs a fund sized on the long case. And when asked to be a trustee, state your duty to all beneficiaries and take advice before saying yes.
terms: Joint action — the general requirement that co-trustees make decisions together unless the deed provides otherwise.
Trustees' resolution — a written record of a decision the trustees have made, used to show authority to third parties.
Beneficial ownership — who ultimately owns or controls an asset, behind the names that appear on the register.

hostile.q: Your ownership chart shows a family trust holding 40 percent of the borrower. Who do I call if something goes wrong, and who signs?
hostile.a: The trustees sign, both of them, as the deed requires, and you will have the deed, their appointments and a resolution authorising each document. For day-to-day matters you call me as managing director of the borrower. If the issue needs a shareholder decision, the trustees decide it, independently, and they have agreed to respond to a lender request within a defined number of business days.
